I sit here with the cursor blinking like a metronome, and the first thing that comes is the sound of rain against the window of a house I no longer live in. That house had a tin roof, and rain on tin is not a sound; it is a conversation. My grandmother used to say the rain was counting the sins of the roof. I never understood if the roof had sinned or if the rain was forgiving it. Now, in this quiet apartment, the rain is just a smear on the glass, silent as a held breath.

What comes next is the smell of coffee from a café in a city I visited once, where the chairs were too small and the waiter had a scar across his eyebrow shaped like a question mark. I remember thinking that everyone in that city walked as if they were late to a funeral, but they were only late to work. The coffee was bitter, and I drank it anyway because leaving it would have been a kind of surrender. I have always been bad at leaving things unfinished. This is probably why I am still writing.

There is a memory of a dog I loved when I was seven. His name was Jasper, and he was the color of toast. He used to wait by the front gate every afternoon at 3:15, not because he could tell time, but because the school bus made a particular wheeze when it turned the corner. Jasper died on a Tuesday, and I learned that grief is just love with nowhere to go. I still think about him when I see a slice of burnt toast. The body keeps inventories of small things.

The instructions said to write whatever comes to me, so I am writing about the way my mother folds towels. She folds them into thirds, then in half, then in half again, and she presses her palm flat on each one as if blessing it. I used to think this was just neatness, but now I understand it is a kind of prayer. She was teaching me order without ever saying the word. I fold my towels the same way now, and sometimes I feel her hand on mine, ghost-like, across two hundred miles.

What comes next is the phrase "the opposite of war is not peace; it is creation." I read that on a poster once in a university hallway. It stayed with me because I have spent most of my life trying to make things—sentences, gardens, friendships—and I have failed at all of them in spectacular ways. But the failing felt less like defeat and more like clearing a throat. Each attempt was a syllable in a longer sentence I am still learning to pronounce.

I am thinking of the first time I saw the ocean. I was twelve, and the water was the color of old glass. My father said, "That's it," as if the ocean needed an introduction. I expected it to roar, but it whispered. It came up to my ankles and then retreated, taking sand from under my feet. I remember the sensation of standing on a world that was slowly being pulled away. I think of that sensation often now, in conversations that shift, in relationships that erode, in the way time moves under me without asking permission.

There is a line from a poem I can't quite remember. It goes something like, "Let the soft animal of your body love what it loves." I think it is Mary Oliver. I think about the soft animal often—the way it wants sleep, warmth, sugar, touch. We spend so much time disciplining the animal, teaching it to sit still, to not want too much, to not flinch. But the animal knows things the mind doesn't. It knows when a room is unsafe. It knows when a person is lying. It knows that the body keeps the score, even if the mind has burned the scoreboard.

I am writing this in a room with a yellow chair. The chair is empty, but it holds the shape of everyone who has sat in it—a ghost of postures. My friend Anna sat there last spring and told me she was leaving her husband. She said, "It's like I've been holding my breath for ten years, and I just remembered how to exhale." I think about that sentence a lot. Exhalation as a form of freedom. We do not talk enough about the violence of holding things in.

What comes next is the memory of a night I spent on a train in a country where I didn't speak the language. The train stopped in the middle of nowhere, and the lights flickered off for a full minute. In that minute, I was certain I had died and this was the afterlife—a dark train car full of strangers, moving nowhere. Then the lights came back, and the woman across from me smiled as if to say, "That happens all the time." It was the most profound thing I have ever experienced for no reason at all.

I am thinking about the word "enough." It is a small word, but it carries the weight of every judgment. Am I writing enough? Am I loving enough? Am I enough? The word is a door that swings both ways. I used to think I needed to be extraordinary to be loved. Now I suspect that being good at being ordinary is its own kind of genius. The people I love most are not the ones who achieved great things; they are the ones who remembered my birthday and asked how I slept and made me tea without being asked. The ordinary is a cathedral if you pay attention.

There is a memory of my grandfather's hands. They were large and cracked, and they smelled of motor oil and mint. He could fix anything—a broken radio, a leaking faucet, a child's heart. He used to say, "Take your time, but don't waste it." I didn't understand the difference until I had children of my own. Taking time is an act of love; wasting it is an act of fear. I am still learning which is which.

I will write about the way light falls on the kitchen table at 5 p.m. in October. It is orange and thin, like watered-down honey. It makes the dust motes look like tiny planets. I used to sit in that light and do my homework, and I believed, with the certainty of childhood, that the world was orderly and that if I did well, good things would follow. I was wrong, but I am not angry. The light is still beautiful, even if it doesn't promise anything.

I am thinking about the future, which is a country I have never visited but whose language I am trying to learn. I practice its conjugations: I will, you will, we will. It is a hopeful grammar. But I also know that the future is just a series of nows wearing a disguise. The only way to arrive is to keep folding towels, keep pouring coffee, keep walking toward the gate at 3:15.

What comes next is the urge to stop. But there is a difference between stopping and finishing. Stopping is an interruption; finishing is a shape. I want this to have a shape. So I will gather the loose threads: rain on tin, Jasper, the yellow chair, the train, the ocean, my grandfather's hands, the word "enough." These are not random. They are the inventory of a life. They are the evidence that even in an ordinary room, on an ordinary day, the mind is a museum with too many wings to count.

I have a few words left. I will use them to say this: if you are reading this, you are not alone. The world is strange and soft and sharp, and we are all just trying to fold our towels, to love our soft animals, to remember how to exhale. The rain will come. The train will stop. The lights will go out and come back on. And someone across from you will smile, as if to say, "That happens all the time." It does. And still, we write. Still, we make. Still, we go on.
